editorial.titleTr: Wordplay on "cutting off Lee Jae-myung"... political disputes must also respect boundaries
summaryTr: ① Lawmaker Ju Jin-woo faced criticism for crossing political lines after using language on social media targeting President Lee Jae-myung.
② Concerns intensified that the expression was inappropriate even with an explanation, given that President Lee Jae-myung faced threats of political terrorism in 2024.
③ As controversy over Lawmaker Lee Jin-sook's tomb visit compounded the situation, calls emerged for politics to be criticized based on facts and evidence while maintaining dignity.

Given that President Lee faced threats from political terrorism in 2024, concerns grew that the expression was inappropriate even with an explanation. Combined with controversy over Representative Lee Jin-sook's visit to a grave site, calls have emerged for politics to be conducted with criticism based on facts and evidence while maintaining dignity.

editorials.titleTr: U.S.-Korea Discord Reflects Alliance Management Failure, Not Submission Issue
summaryTr: It is problematic to view Korean-American tensions simply as a matter of submission controversy.
The government's ideological disposition has led to failures in alliance management.
With communication channels to the United States severed, a review of pragmatic diplomacy is urgently needed.
editorials.bodyTr: The editorial pointed out that viewing the Korea-U.S. conflict solely through the lens of submission and dependency arguments oversimplifies the problem. The editorial argued that ideological perceptions held by some government officials led to failures in alliance management, widening discord between Korea and the United States. The editorial stressed that as communication with the United States has reached its limits and information-sharing cooperation has stalled, practical diplomacy requires review, noting that discussions on nuclear energy agreements and nuclear-powered submarines have also come to a halt.

LH has achieved only one-quarter of its public housing construction targets, and the article argues that the organization should focus on expanding supply.

editorial.body: 입력 종합 26면 강경화 주미 한국대사가 그제(12일) 국감에서 작금의 한·미 관계의 가장 어려운 현안이 정보 협력이라고 했다. 지난달 한·미 외교장관회담에서 “정보 협력에 문제가 있다”는 마코 루비오 국무장관의 말을 전하며 “아직 미국이 기대하는 만큼 문제가 충분히 해소됐다고 생각하지 않는다”고 평가했다. 올 3월 정동영 통일부 장관이 평북 구성의 우라늄 농축시설 발언을 한 뒤 6개월 넘게 이어져 온 정보 공유 제한을 둘러싼 갈등이 장기화하고 있는 것이다. 강 대사는 이날 미 측의 기대가 무엇인지는 답변을 피했다. 하지만 미국이 ‘이미 공개된 정보’ 또는 ‘사실관계 착오’라는 이재명 대통령과 정 장관의 입장을 납득하지 않고 있다는 점은 분명하다. 문제가 해소되지 않은 여파로 국가정보원 직원의 비자 발급이 지연되고, 그간 한·미·일 협력을 강조해 온 미 측이 최근 3국 실무회의에서 국정원을 배제한 것이다. 이런 상황에서 어제 이 대통령의 국무회의 발언은 여러모로 사태 해결에 도움이 되지 못한다. 이 대통령은 “대한민국의 외교 방침은 실용적 국익 외교”라며 “국익을 지키는 외교를 해야 하며, 국가 간 관계에 있어 굴종적·사대적 태도를 지양해야 한다”고 했다. 그 사례로 대미 투자 프로젝트를 들었다. 그러나 서로 주고받는 협상 영역인 통상 분야와는 달리, 안보 관련 한·미 정보 공유 제한의 피해는 고스란히 한국이 받는다. 정보를 제때 공유받지 못하면 한국의 국익에 손상이 갈 수밖에 없다. 나아가 강 대사는 “백악관 고위급 협의가 답답할 정도로 이뤄지지 않고 있다”고 했다. 우리 주미 대사가 백악관과 소통에 어려움을 겪고 있는 것이 한·미 관계의 현주소다. 이번 사태가 심각한 것은 철통 같은 동맹인 양국이 상호 불신으로 치닫고 있기 때문이다. 미 측으로선 자신들이 제공한 정보를 한국이 어떻게 활용할지를 신뢰할 수 없다는 것이다. 이 대통령은 “우리를 둘러싼 주변 강국과의 관계 관리도 여전히 중요하다”고 했다. 중국·러시아와의 관계를 말한 것이겠지만 같은 말도 발언의 상황에 따라 맥락이 달라진다. 현 상황에서는 미국의 불신을 증폭시킬 소지가 다분하다. 정부의 상황 인식과 대응이 과연 실용적 접근인지, 또 국익을 위한 것인지 묻지 않을 수 없다.

editorial.titleTr: [Editorial] Restoring Korea-U.S. Intelligence Cooperation Serves National Interest and Pragmatism
summaryTr: The breakdown of South Korea-U.S. intelligence cooperation has emerged as the top issue facing the Korea-U.S. alliance.
The conflict has persisted for more than six months since the March remarks on enriched uranium.
The government's emphasis on pragmatic diplomacy is instead amplifying American distrust.
editorial.bodyTr: Ambassador to the United States Kang Kyung-wha stated during a parliamentary audit two days ago that information cooperation is currently the most pressing issue in Korea-U.S. relations. She relayed remarks by Secretary of State Marco Rubio at last month's Korea-U.S. foreign minister talks stating "there are problems in intelligence cooperation," and assessed that "the U.S. does not yet believe the issues have been sufficiently resolved to meet its expectations." A conflict over restricted information sharing that has persisted for more than six months since Unification Minister Jung Dong-young's March remarks about uranium enrichment facilities in Kusong, North Pyongan Province, continues to fester. Ambassador Kang avoided answering what the U.S. side's expectations are. However, it is clear that the United States is not accepting President Lee Jae-myung and Minister Jung's position that the information was "already public" or a "factual error." As a consequence of the unresolved issue, visa issuance for National Intelligence Service personnel has been delayed, and the U.S. side, which has emphasized trilateral Korea-U.S.-Japan cooperation, recently excluded the NIS from trilateral working-level meetings. Against this backdrop, President Lee's remarks at a state affairs meeting yesterday do little to help resolve the situation. The president stated, "the Republic of Korea's diplomatic policy is pragmatic national interest diplomacy," and emphasized that "we must pursue diplomacy that protects national interests and abandon subservient and dependent attitudes in relations between nations." He cited U.S. investment projects as an example. However, unlike trade, which is a reciprocal negotiation arena, the damage from restricted Korea-U.S. intelligence sharing in security matters falls entirely on South Korea. If Korea fails to receive information in a timely manner, it inevitably incurs damage to national interests. Moreover, Ambassador Kang stated that "high-level consultations with the White House are frustratingly infrequent." Our ambassador to Washington struggling to communicate with the White House reflects the current state of Korea-U.S. relations. This situation is serious because the two allies are moving toward mutual distrust. The U.S. side cannot trust how Korea will utilize information it provides. President Lee stated that "managing relations with neighboring powers surrounding us remains important." While he was referring to relations with China and Russia, the same words carry different implications depending on the context of their utterance. In the current situation, there is considerable potential to amplify American distrust. One cannot help but question whether the government's situational awareness and response represent a truly pragmatic approach and whether they genuinely serve the national interest.

editorial.title: Shift in tides
editorial.body: EU-China hybrid deal exposes weaknesses in Korea’s low-tariff automotive market Protectionist barriers rarely eliminate market distortions; they often redirect the pressure elsewhere. As major economic blocs close their doors to Chinese vehicles, South Korea could face an influx of rerouted exports, leaving domestic automakers to compete on uneven terms. The European Union’s agreement with Beijing on Friday shows how quickly the ground is shifting. The deal aims to halve Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid exports to the bloc over the next four years, as European officials seek to protect an automotive industry under mounting pressure. Chinese brands accounted for 25 percent of the EU’s hybrid market in the first half of this year, up from 2 percent in 2024. Brussels had imposed additional duties on Chinese electric vehicles, taking the total levy to as much as 45.3 percent, while hybrids faced only the standard 10 percent tariff. Chinese manufacturers exploited the gap, cutting prices and gaining ground. The US has imposed tariffs of up to 127.5 percent on Chinese electric vehicles, and Japan has used subsidies to support its own industry. Despite their different approaches, both governments are seeking to shield local manufacturers from Chinese competition. These barriers could redirect Chinese exports toward other markets. Chinese automakers face weak demand at home and mounting barriers in major export markets. As Europe narrows one route, manufacturers have a stronger incentive to seek markets where entry remains relatively easy. Korea is one such destination. Its standard 8 percent tariff on imported passenger vehicles is lower than China’s 15 percent duty on imported cars. The gap reflects Seoul’s long-standing interest in keeping overseas markets accessible to local exporters. Yet a policy designed to secure foreign market access leaves domestic producers exposed when trading partners offer their own manufacturers greater protection. Chinese brands are already gaining ground here. New registrations of Chinese-brand electric vehicles reached 12,178 in the first half of this year, up 334.6 percent from a year earlier. BYD registered 20,137 vehicles from January through September, ranking fourth among imported-car sellers. The challenge for Hyundai Motor and Kia is especially acute as competition extends into hybrids, a segment in which both companies have invested heavily. Hyundai’s global sales fell 7 percent in the first nine months of the year, while domestic sales dropped 16.3 percent. Its first-half operating profit also declined 25.8 percent year on year. Sales figures show that Chinese rivals are gaining a greater share as Korean automakers contend with weaker sales and margin pressure. New tariffs may appear to be the quickest answer, but they would invite legal and diplomatic complications under World Trade Organization rules and the Korea-China free trade agreement. Retaliation could also reach exporters in sectors far removed from automobiles. Seoul needs a response that strengthens local production without jeopardizing access to overseas markets. The immediate gap is domestic support. The government’s domestic production tax credit covers batteries but excludes electric vehicles, the finished products those batteries power. That omission weakens the incentive to manufacture in Korea just as foreign governments are backing their own industries. Seoul should reconsider the exclusion and extend targeted assistance to research, factory investment and critical supply chains. The aim should be to improve the conditions under which Korean-made vehicles compete, not to promise shelter from competition. Local manufacturers depend on access to overseas markets, and a blunt tariff response could undermine that advantage. An open market, however, needs a coherent industrial policy to sustain the domestic production base on which export competitiveness rests. Trade barriers rarely contain competitive pressure within the markets where they are erected. Unless Seoul strengthens the foundations of automotive production at home, the country may find itself absorbing a larger share of the adjustment imposed by others. 보호주의적 장벽은 시장 왜곡을 제거하기보다는 압력을 다른 곳으로 전가하는 경우가 많다. 주요 경제권이 중국 자동차에 대한 문을 닫으면서 한국은 우회 수출의 유입으로 인해 국내 자동차 제조사들이 불공정한 조건에서 경쟁해야 할 상황에 직면할 수 있다. 유럽연합이 금요일 베이징과 체결한 협상은 상황이 얼마나 빠르게 변하고 있는지 보여준다. 이 협상은 앞으로 4년간 중국의 하이브리드 및 플러그인 하이브리드 자동차 수출을 절반으로 줄이는 것을 목표로 하고 있으며, 유럽 관계자들은 증가하는 압력을 받고 있는 자동차 산업을 보호하려 하고 있다. 중국 브랜드가 올해 상반기 EU의 하이브리드 시장에서 25%를 차지했으며, 이는 2024년의 2%에서 증가한 수치다. 브뤼셀은 중국 전기자동차에 추가 관세를 부과해 총 관세를 45.3%까지 높였던 반면, 하이브리드는 표준 10% 관세만 적용받았다. 중국 제조사들은 이 간격을 이용해 가격을 인하하고 시장 점유율을 높였다. 미국은 중국 전기자동차에 최대 127.5%의 관세를 부과했으며, 일본은 자국 산업을 지원하기 위해 보조금을 사용했다. 접근 방식은 다르지만 두 정부 모두 중국의 경쟁으로부터 국내 제조사를 보호하려고 하고 있다. 이러한 장벽들은 중국의 수출을 다른 시장으로 돌릴 수 있다. 중국 자동차 제조사들은 국내 수요 부진과 주요 수출 시장의 증가하는 장벽에 직면해 있다. 유럽이 한 경로를 좁혀지면서 제조사들은 진입이 여전히 상대적으로 용이한 시장을 찾을 인센티브를 갖게 된다. 한국이 그러한 시장 중 하나다. 한국의 수입 승용차에 대한 표준 관세율은 8%로 중국의 수입차 15% 관세보다 낮다. 이러한 격차는 서울의 해외 시장을 국내 수출업체에게 개방된 상태로 유지하려는 오랜 관심을 반영한다. 그러나 외국 시장 접근을 확보하기 위해 설계된 정책은 거래 상대국이 자국 제조사에 더 큰 보호를 제공할 때 국내 생산자들을 노출시킨다. 중국 브랜드는 이미 이곳에서 점유율을 높이고 있다. 올해 상반기 중국 브랜드 전기자동차의 신규 등록은 12,178대로 전년 대비 334.6% 증가했다. editorials.title: Shift in tides
editorials.body: EU-China hybrid deal exposes weaknesses in Korea’s low-tariff automotive market Protectionist barriers rarely eliminate market distortions; they often redirect the pressure elsewhere. As major economic blocs close their doors to Chinese vehicles, South Korea could face an influx of rerouted exports, leaving domestic automakers to compete on uneven terms. The European Union’s agreement with Beijing on Friday shows how quickly the ground is shifting. The deal aims to halve Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid exports to the bloc over the next four years, as European officials seek to protect an automotive industry under mounting pressure. Chinese brands accounted for 25 percent of the EU’s hybrid market in the first half of this year, up from 2 percent in 2024. Brussels had imposed additional duties on Chinese electric vehicles, taking the total levy to as much as 45.3 percent, while hybrids faced only the standard 10 percent tariff. Chinese manufacturers exploited the gap, cutting prices and gaining ground. The US has imposed tariffs of up to 127.5 percent on Chinese electric vehicles, and Japan has used subsidies to support its own industry. Despite their different approaches, both governments are seeking to shield local manufacturers from Chinese competition. These barriers could redirect Chinese exports toward other markets. Chinese automakers face weak demand at home and mounting barriers in major export markets. As Europe narrows one route, manufacturers have a stronger incentive to seek markets where entry remains relatively easy. Korea is one such destination. Its standard 8 percent tariff on imported passenger vehicles is lower than China’s 15 percent duty on imported cars. The gap reflects Seoul’s long-standing interest in keeping overseas markets accessible to local exporters. Yet a policy designed to secure foreign market access leaves domestic producers exposed when trading partners offer their own manufacturers greater protection. Chinese brands are already gaining ground here. New registrations of Chinese-brand electric vehicles reached 12,178 in the first half of this year, up 334.6 percent from a year earlier. BYD registered 20,137 vehicles from January through September, ranking fourth among imported-car sellers. The challenge for Hyundai Motor and Kia is especially acute as competition extends into hybrids, a segment in which both companies have invested heavily. Hyundai’s global sales fell 7 percent in the first nine months of the year, while domestic sales dropped 16.3 percent. Its first-half operating profit also declined 25.8 percent year on year. Sales figures show that Chinese rivals are gaining a greater share as Korean automakers contend with weaker sales and margin pressure. New tariffs may appear to be the quickest answer, but they would invite legal and diplomatic complications under World Trade Organization rules and the Korea-China free trade agreement. Retaliation could also reach exporters in sectors far removed from automobiles. Seoul needs a response that strengthens local production without jeopardizing access to overseas markets. The immediate gap is domestic support. The government’s domestic production tax credit covers batteries but excludes electric vehicles, the finished products those batteries power. That omission weakens the incentive to manufacture in Korea just as foreign governments are backing their own industries. Seoul should reconsider the exclusion and extend targeted assistance to research, factory investment and critical supply chains. The aim should be to improve the conditions under which Korean-made vehicles compete, not to promise shelter from competition. Local manufacturers depend on access to overseas markets, and a blunt tariff response could undermine that advantage. An open market, however, needs a coherent industrial policy to sustain the domestic production base on which export competitiveness rests. Trade barriers rarely contain competitive pressure within the markets where they are erected. Unless Seoul strengthens the foundations of automotive production at home, the country may find itself absorbing a larger share of the adjustment imposed by others. summaryTr: AI-equipped smart glasses were detected as cheating devices in entrance exams at Yonsei University and Seoul City University.

Analog-style proctoring has revealed its limitations in detecting advanced technological cheating methods.
editorials.bodyTr:
Students wearing AI-equipped smart glasses have been caught repeatedly during the College Scholastic Ability Test essay portions at Yonsei University and the University of Seoul. This marks the first confirmed case of cheating using smart glasses in domestic university admissions. With the College Scholastic Ability Test scheduled for next month and numerous early admission deadlines ahead, measures to prevent cheating must be strengthened immediately.

The incident is deeply troubling for several reasons. Smart glasses equipped with artificial intelligence are high-tech devices that can transmit test questions in real time and receive answers through wireless networks. If students use such devices, it essentially nullifies the fairness of the exam. The fact that multiple students attempted this suggests they obtained information about how to use these devices and may have even received answers from outside sources. This points to a organized, premeditated scheme rather than an isolated incident.

What is more alarming is that these devices managed to evade detection at the gate. Universities have security checkpoints where students are screened with metal detectors and bag inspections. Yet smart glasses, which resemble regular eyewear, slipped through. This exposes critical vulnerabilities in the current security system. As technology advances, cheating methods will only become more sophisticated. Universities must upgrade their screening procedures accordingly.

The authorities must also investigate whether there is an organized network behind these incidents. If private institutions or individuals are profiting by providing smart glasses and answers to test-takers, this constitutes a serious crime that warrants criminal charges. The scope and scale of the cheating network must be thoroughly revealed.

Controversy over negative perceptions toward large corporations is spreading.
editorials.bodyTr: Controversy is mounting over Fair Trade Commission Chairman Ju Byung-ki's negative perception of large corporations. When questioned during a National Assembly audit on the 12th about his past remarks and articles, including "conglomerates exploit South Korea" and "the enemy creating an exploitative South Korea is the hereditary economy of conglomerates and large business groups," Chairman Ju responded, "While the expression is rhetorical and somewhat excessive, I still think that way.
